reason: The cited evidence (E1–E5) comes entirely from a single room-temperature cyclic salt spray study on passivated Q235 steel. It describes film rupture, rust layer formation, and corrosion stages at ambient temperature, but provides no data on high-temperature (700–900 °C) exposure, thermal stress effects, or enhanced chloride mobility. The key premises about high-temperature degradation mechanisms are therefore unsupported by the cited passages.
premises: Pre-passivated Q235 steel has an initially uniform, adherent passivation film that provides electrochemical protection at room temperature.
High-temperature (700–900 °C) aggressive salt exposure induces thermal stresses and enhanced chloride mobility that embrittle and rupture the film.
Film rupture converts the passivation film into a porous, nonprotective iron oxide scale.
This degradation triggers localized, accelerated corrosion with significant weight loss and pitting.
